stem: A company runs an API on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The group is attached to a target group of an Application Load Balancer and keeps its default health check settings. After some days of running, a memory leak makes the API on some instances return HTTP 503 errors. The target group marks these instances as unhealthy, but they stay in the group, and the other instances become overloaded. The company must ensure that such instances are replaced automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: keeps its default health check settings
The target group marks these instances as unhealthy, but they stay in the group

options.text: Configure the target group to terminate each instance that fails its health checks, so that the Auto Scaling group launches a new instance in its place.
options.why: A failed check makes the load balancer [stop routing requests to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-elb-requests-before-detection-fail); replacing the instance is work for the group.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EBS health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also replaces each instance whose API returns HTTP 503 errors.
options.why: EBS health checks test whether volumes are reachable and [passing I/O status checks](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-ebs-check-must-be-turned-on); a leaking API on a healthy volume passes them.
options.misconception: believes that EBS health checks test the application on the instance

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that the group also acts on the health that the load balancer reports.
options.why: With this setting, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace) and [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), with no code to run.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the unhealthy host count of the target group that invokes an AWS Lambda function to mark each failing instance unhealthy.
options.why: It works through [SetInstanceHealth](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-set-instance-health-custom-check), but an alarm and a function are more to build and run than one group setting.

explanation: The API fails while each instance keeps running, so the EC2 status checks still pass. By default the group [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, so unhealthy targets stay in it. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on); then the group marks such an instance unhealthy [on its next periodic health check](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-unhealthy-replaced) and replaces it.
takeaway: When the load balancer sees a failure that the EC2 checks miss, turn on the ELB health check type.
twin: If the stem said "the group has no load balancer, and the worker process crashes" instead: a custom health check, because the group [only replaces instances that are unhealthy or unreachable](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-default-ec2-checks-only) by the EC2 checks.
say: The group ignores the load balancer checks until you turn them on, so I'd turn on ELB health checks.

stem: A company runs a web application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The application keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies. During the day the load changes often, and at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%. Users then see slow responses. The company expects the number of users to grow during the next year. The application must handle the growth and the daily peaks with minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: keeps its state in memory and cannot run as several copies
at peaks the CPU utilization of the instance reaches 100%

options.text: Change the instance to a larger instance type with more vCPUs and more memory, and move to a larger type again each time the load grows.
options.why: This application runs as one copy, so a larger type is the way to add vCPUs; [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) to resize it, so plan each stop outside the peaks.

options.text: Turn on detailed monitoring for the instance, so that Amazon CloudWatch publishes the CPU utilization metric every minute instead of every five minutes.
options.why: Detailed monitoring reports the metric more often, but it adds no capacity, so the single instance still runs out of CPU at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that more frequent metrics add capacity

options.text: Run the application in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, with a target tracking scaling policy on CPU utilization.
options.why: An Auto Scaling group runs several copies of the application, but this application keeps its state in the memory of one copy.
options.misconception: believes that every application can run as several copies behind a load balancer

options.text: Attach a second elastic network interface to the instance, so that the instance can accept twice as many user requests during the peaks.
options.why: A second network interface adds a network path, not vCPUs, so the CPU utilization of the single instance still reaches 100% at the peaks.
options.misconception: believes that a second network interface adds compute capacity

explanation: This application keeps its state in the memory of one instance and runs as one copy, so a group of several instances does not fit. More CPU and memory come from a larger instance type. To change the type, [you must stop your instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required), so [plan for downtime](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-vertical-stop-required) and resize outside the daily peaks.
takeaway: When the application runs as one copy, scale up to a larger type and plan a stop for each resize.
twin: If the stem said "stateless web application" instead: an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, because adding instances is [essential for dynamic workloads with fluctuating demands](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-decision-guide-horizontal-for-fluctuating).
say: It keeps its state in one copy, so I'd move to a larger instance type and plan a short stop.

stem: A company created an Auto Scaling group with the AWS CLI and later turned on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for it. The group runs a web application behind an Application Load Balancer. The application needs about 4 minutes after launch before it answers the target group health checks. Now each new instance is terminated and replaced again and again, so the group does not reach its desired capacity. Instances whose application fails later must still be replaced. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: created an Auto Scaling group with the AWS CLI

options.text: Increase the default cooldown of the group, so that the group waits longer before it replaces an instance that fails its health checks.
options.why: The group [does not wait for the cooldown period](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-cooldown-unhealthy-replacement-does-not-wait) before it replaces an unhealthy instance, so a longer cooldown changes nothing here.
options.misconception: believes that the cooldown delays the replacement of unhealthy instances

options.text: Change the health check type of the group back to Amazon EC2 status checks only, so that the group ignores the target group results.
options.why: It stops the loop, but the group then [only replaces instances that are unhealthy or unreachable](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lb-default-ec2-checks-only) by the EC2 checks, so a failed application stays.
options.misconception: believes that the EC2 status checks also find a failed application

options.text: Add a launch lifecycle hook, and change the user data script so that it completes the lifecycle action when the application answers requests.
options.why: It works, because with launch hooks you can [set the health check grace period to 0](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-zero-with-launch-hooks), but it changes the script and adds a hook to manage.

options.text: Set the health check grace period of the group to a value that is longer than the time that the application needs to start.
options.why: The group runs the ELB checks on a new instance [after a grace period](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-optional-checks-after-grace-period), so a period that covers the start ends the loop and keeps the checks.

explanation: A group created with the AWS CLI starts with a grace period of [0 seconds](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-console-300-cli-0). The ELB checks then start at once, the target group reports each new instance as unhealthy before the application answers, and the group [terminates the unhealthy instance and launches another](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-unhealthy-terminated-replaced). A grace period longer than the 4-minute start breaks the loop and keeps the ELB checks on.
takeaway: Set a grace period that covers the application start; with the AWS CLI it starts at [0 seconds](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-grace-period-console-300-cli-0).
twin: If the stem said "new instances receive requests before the application is ready" instead: a launch lifecycle hook, because it holds the instance until it is [ready to accept traffic](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-lifecycle-hook-lb-registration).
say: A CLI-made group has no grace period, so I'd set one that covers the four-minute start.
